description: We are QUBIT, a team from Cochabamba, Bolivia
summary:
Yaku is a mobile-friendly web app that helps farmers in Cochabamba answer two practical questions: Will my crop have enough water, and what could I plant after harvest?

Farmers mark their field on a map. Yaku combines NASA satellite estimates of soil moisture and past rainfall, NASA POWER climate records, SoilGrids data on how much water the soil can hold, and Open-Meteo forecasts. It uses these inputs to estimate when a crop might run short of water and how much extra water it could need.

To explore what to plant next, farmers enter just their current crop and expected harvest date. Yaku compares up to three alternatives, shows estimated planting and harvest dates, and provides a downloadable summary. It also uses Cochabamba’s official drainage maps to flag places worth inspecting when heavy rain is expected. The goal is to help farmers plan irrigation and choose their next crop with clearer information about the water available to them.
details:
Yaku helps farmers in Cochabamba make two decisions about their own fields: whether their current crop may need more water, and what they could plant after harvest. Farmers can mark a location or draw their field on a map and open a report on their phone without creating an account.

For irrigation planning, Yaku combines NASA SMAP soil moisture estimates, NASA IMERG rainfall observations, SoilGrids estimates of soil water retention, and Open-Meteo forecasts. A daily water balance uses FAO-56 crop coefficients to estimate when the crop might run short of water and how much extra water it could need. Farmers can review the next 7 or 14 days and see how delaying an irrigation turn could affect the crop. When a field location overlaps a drainage area mapped by the municipality and the app detects heavy rainfall, Yaku can generate a field inspection checklist.

For planting decisions, farmers enter only their current crop and expected harvest date. Yaku uses NASA POWER climate records, crop reference data, and the available soil profile to compare up to three alternatives. Each option shows estimated planting and harvest dates, possible days with water stress, and how much additional water the crop could need. Farmers can download the results as a PDF to discuss with a grower, technician, or irrigation group.

We built Yaku with TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Leaflet, with PostgreSQL for saved parcels and Docker for local deployment. We designed the interface around decisions farmers already make, with a mobile layout, crop photos, and plain-language results. We also considered patchy connectivity and gaps in regional data. The app retains selected information for offline viewing and explains when the available data are insufficient for a calculation.
